'''Ruth Hubbard''' (March 3, 1924 – September 1, 2016) was a professor of biology at [[Harvard University]], where she was the first woman to hold a [[academic tenure|tenure]]d professorship position in biology.<ref name=cambridgeforum>{{cite web|url=http://www.harvardsquarelibrary.org/cfs/ruth_hubbard.php |title=Ruth Hubbard |work=Cambridge Forum Speakers 1970–1990 |access-date=November 29, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120405051022/http://www.harvardsquarelibrary.org/cfs/ruth_hubbard.php |archive-date=April 5, 2012 |publisher=Harvard Square Library}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite journal | last1 = Holloway | first1 = M | year = 1995 | title = Profile: Ruth Hubbard – Turning the Inside Out | journal = [[Scientific American]] | volume = 272 | issue = 6| pages = 49–50 | doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0695-49| bibcode = 1995SciAm.272f..49H}}</ref>

During her active research career from the 1940s to the 1960s, she made important contributions to the understanding of the biochemistry and [[photochemistry]] of vision in [[vertebrate]]s and [[invertebrate]]s.<ref name=cambridgeforum/> In 1967, Hubbard and [[George Wald]] shared the [[Paul Karrer Gold Medal]] for their work in this area.<ref name=cambridgeforum/>

In the late 1960s, her interests shifted from science to societal issues and activism.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Barr|first=Dorothy|date=2018-01-02|title=Profiles in Science for Science Librarians: Ruth Hubbard, Scientist and Social Activist|journal=Science & Technology Libraries|volume=37|issue=1|pages=63–70|doi=10.1080/0194262X.2017.1395722|s2cid=64720881|issn=0194-262X|url=http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:41017646|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
In 1924, Hubbard was born Ruth Hoffmann in Vienna, Austria.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hubbard, Ruth, 1924–. Papers of Ruth Hubbard, 1920–2007|url=http://oasis.lib.harvard.edu/oasis/deliver/~sch01418|website=oasis.lib.harvard.edu|publisher=President and Fellows of Harvard College|access-date=January 26, 2015}}</ref> Her parents, Richard Hoffmann and Helene Ehrlich Hoffmann, were both physicians and leftist intellectuals.<ref name=":2">Sarah Corbett, ''[https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2016/12/21/magazine/the-lives-they-lived-ruth-hubbard.html The lives they lives: Ruth Hubbard]'', [[New York Times]], December 21, 2016</ref> Her mother was also a concert-quality pianist, and as a child, Ruth showed promise on the piano as well.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.meaningfulfunerals.net/obituary/3875903?lud=20501CE3BC2F0630A8B17BF63879DAF7&fh_id=14764|title=Obituary for Ruth Wald at ANDERSON-BRYANT FUNERAL HOME|website=www.meaningfulfunerals.net|language=en|access-date=2019-03-16}}</ref> When Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938, the Hoffmanns immigrated to the United States to escape.<ref name=HowStuffWorks>{{cite web|title=Ruth Hubbard|date=October 21, 2008|url=http://science.howstuffworks.com/dictionary/famous-scientists/biologists/ruth-hubbard-info.htm|publisher=HowStuffWorks (Discovery Communications)|access-date=January 27, 2011}}</ref> The family settled first in [[Brookline, Massachusetts]], where Ruth graduated [[Brookline High School]], and then in Cambridge.

Ruth decided to enroll at Radcliffe College with the intent to pursue a pre-medicine degree, which she attributes to the fact that everyone around her was a doctor.<ref name=":0" /> At that time, Radcliffe was a sister institution to Harvard since women were not yet allowed to enroll at the university. Ruth sensed the disdain that the distinguished Harvard professors had for the system that required them to travel to the Radcliffe campus to teach the small female classes after teaching the same lecture to their male students at Harvard.<ref name=":2" /> However, by 1946 most classes were [[Mixed-sex education|coeducational]] and taught by Harvard professors.<ref name=":1" /> For a brief period, Ruth was interested in pursuing a degree in Philosophy and Physics, and even though she was never explicitly told not to go into Physics, she got the feeling that she was not welcome. She attributes this feeling of unease to the time that she took a coeducational Physics course in which she was only one of two women in the class of 350 students.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Ruth finally settled on biochemical sciences, and in 1944 graduated from Radcliffe College with a B.A. in biochemical sciences.<ref name="HowStuffWorks" />

Out of a desire to help the Allied War effort in [[World War II]], Ruth joined the laboratory of George Wald, where they conducted research on infrared vision. She briefly relocated to [[Chattanooga]] where her first husband Frank Hubbard was stationed. When the war ended, they returned to Cambridge. Ruth returned to Radcliffe in 1946 in pursuit of her doctorate in biology.<ref name=":0" /> She was awarded a predoctoral fellowship by the [[U.S. Public Health Service]] in 1948, allowing her to study at the University College Hospital Medical School in London. Ruth received her PhD in biology in 1950.<ref name="HowStuffWorks" />

==Scientific career==
After receiving her PhD from Harvard, Ruth became a research fellow. She worked under [[George Wald]], investigating the [[biochemistry]] of [[retinal]] and [[retinol]].<ref name="dowling2">{{cite book|chapter-url=https://www.nap.edu/catalog/9977/biographical-memoirs-v78|title=Biographical Memoirs. Volume 78|last1=Dowling|first1=John E.|date=2000|publisher=National Academies Press|isbn=9780309070355|location=Washington|pages=299–317|chapter=George Wald}}</ref> According to an interview given by Ruth, together they built on the work that Wald had researched during a fellowship following his own doctorate degree. He had confirmed the long-held belief that [[vitamin A]] was related to [[Visual perception|vision]]. Not only did he find that light absorption liberated vitamin A, he also found an intermediate of the visual pigment [[rhodopsin]] and vitamin A. This intermediate was the base of Ruth’s early work, where she attempted to determine the chemistry of the rhodopsin cycle.<ref name=":3">{{cite web|url=http://www.prx.org/pieces/41030-episode-19-ruth-hubbard#description|title=How to Think About Science: Episode 19 – Ruth Hubbard|publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation via Public Radio Exchange (PRX)|access-date=January 27, 2011}}</ref> In 1952, Ruth received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen, Denmark.<ref name="HowStuffWorks" /> Wald shared the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] in 1967 for his discoveries about how the eye works.<ref name=":3" /> In the same year, the pair was awarded the Paul Karrer Gold Medal specifically for their work with rhodopsin.<ref name=":2" />

Hubbard made many important contributions to the visual sciences but her single most important contribution was that visual excitation is initiated by a chemical rearrangement of the visual pigment (rhodopsin) which is called a cis-trans [[isomerization]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=George |last1=Wald|author-link1=George Wald|first2= Paul K.|last2= Brown|first3= Ruth|last3= Hubbard|first4=William |last4= Oroshnik|title= Hindered cis isomers of vitamin A and retinene: The structure of the neo-B isomer |pmid= 16589696 |pmc= 528115 |year=1956|journal= [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |volume=  41 |issue= 7 |pages=438–451 |doi=10.1073/pnas.41.7.438|bibcode=1955PNAS...41..438W|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=n1>{{cite retinene [[isomerase]] (now called [[RPE65]]) that converts all-trans retinal (the post-illumination form) back into 11-cis retinal. She also studied the visual pigments in several new species.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=George|last1= Wald|author-link1=George Wald|first2= Ruth|last2= Hubbard |title=Visual pigment of a decapod crustacean: The lobster|year=1957|journal= Nature |volume=180|issue=4580|pages= 278–280|doi=10.1038/180278a0|pmid= 13464816|bibcode=1957Natur.180..278W|s2cid= 4163928}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=Ruth|last1= Hubbard|first2= George|last2= Wald|author-link2=George Wald |title=Visual pigment of the horseshoe crab, ''Limulus polyphemus'' |journal=Nature |volume=186|issue=4720 |pages= 212–215|doi=10.1038/186212b0|pmid= 13852541|year=1960 |bibcode=1960Natur.186..212H |s2cid= 1620108}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first1=Linda |last1=Sperling|first2=Ruth |last2=Hubbard|title=Squid retinochrome|year=1975|pmid=235007|pmc=2214869|journal=[[The Journal of General Physiology]]|volume=65|issue=2|pages= 235–251 |doi=10.1085/jgp.65.2.235}}</ref> Her early work focused on the basic properties of rhodopsin, which is a combination of the [[chromophore]] (retinal) and a protein called opsin, which is reutilized in the resynthesis of rhodopsin. Hubbard published at least 31 scientific papers devoted to vision.

==Social commentary and political activity==
In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Hubbard became interested in social and political dimensions of biological issues. In her book ''The Politics of Women's Biology'', she wrote that she had been a "devout scientist" from 1947 until the late 1960s, but the [[Vietnam War]] and the [[women's liberation movement]] led her to change her priorities.

Hubbard describes an instance where she was working with squid as one of the pivotal moments where her interests shifted from scientific research to social relevance. Despite working with squid, cattle, and frogs for years when researching the complexities of vision, at that instant it suddenly began to bother her. She said, “I began to have the feeling that nothing I could find out was worth killing another squid.”<ref name=":0" />

Around the same time in the late 1960s, as a member of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, Ruth was asked to give a talk about being a female in the sciences. While conducting interviews of her fellow female scientists, Hubbard discovered that they were all in similar situations. Each of the women were accomplished in their fields, yet none of them had real jobs.<ref name=":0" /> They all had what Ruth called “nonjobs.” They had titles such as lecturer or associate which meant they had little to no job security, while their male-counterparts were either on the path to professorships or had already received tenure.<ref name=":3" /> This led Ruth and others to join a group that petitioned Harvard to reevaluate the job statuses of its female faculty. Ruth Hubbard was the first woman to be offered a tenured Harvard professorship in the Biology Department in 1973.<ref name=":0" />

After being promoted in 1973 from what she called the "typical women's ghetto" of "research associate and lecturer" positions to a tenured faculty position at Harvard, she felt increased freedom to pursue new interests.<ref>Ruth Hubbard (1990), ''The Politics of Women's Biology'', Rutgers University Press. pp. 1–2. {{ISBN|0-8135-1490-8}}.</ref>

One such interest manifested itself in the new seminar course she taught at Harvard titled “Biology 109 - Biology and Women’s Issues.”<ref name=":1" /> The class looked at the role of women in science and how the absence of women in scientific fields had affected the scientific questions that were asked.<ref name=":2" />

In the late 1980s and 1990s, Ruth gave several interviews challenging the power structure in STEM fields. What constitutes science, she told the Globe in 1990, usually is decided by “a self-perpetuating, self-reflexive group: by the chosen for the chosen,” and those “chosen” historically were upper-class white men.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2016/09/04/ruth-hubbard-first-woman-tenured-biology-harvard/zdiRSECiShE4rAJaCBNNTP/story.html|title=Ruth Hubbard, 92, first woman tenured in biology at Harvard - The Boston Globe|last=Reporter|first=Bryan Marquard-|website=BostonGlobe.com|access-date=2019-03-16}}</ref> “Women and nonwhite, working-class and poor men have largely been outside the process of science-making,” Dr. Hubbard told The New York Times in 1981. “Though we have been described by scientists, by and large we have not been the describers and definers of scientific reality. We have not formulated the questions scientists ask, nor have we answered them. This undoubtedly has affected the content of science, but it has also affected the social context and the ambience in which science is done.”<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/11/23/us/scholars-face-a-challenge-by-feminists.html|title=Scholars Face a Challenge by Feminists|last=Fiske|first=Edward B.|date=1981-11-23|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-03-16|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

She became known as a strong critic of [[sociobiology]]. Geneticist [[Richard Lewontin]] has said, "No one has been a more influential critic of the biological theory of women's inequality than Ruth Hubbard."<ref>[http://dssmhi1.fas.harvard.edu/emuseumdev/code/emuseum.asp?action=advsearch&newsearch=1&profile=people&rawsearch=constituentid/,/is/,/7661/,/false/,/true&style=single&searchdesc=Ruth%20Hubbard Ruth Hubbard] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120318160021/http://dssmhi1.fas.harvard.edu/emuseumdev/code/emuseum.asp?action=advsearch&newsearch=1&profile=people&rawsearch=constituentid%2F%2C%2Fis%2F%2C%2F7661%2F%2C%2Ffalse%2F%2C%2Ftrue&style=single&searchdesc=Ruth%20Hubbard |date=March 18, 2012 }}, Harvard University Department of the History of Science, web content accessed July 27, 2011</ref> In a 2006 essay entitled "Race and Genes," she wrote:

<blockquote>It is beyond comprehension, in this century which has witnessed holocausts of ethnic, racial, and religious extermination in many parts of our planet, perpetrated by peoples of widely different cultural and political affiliations and beliefs, that educated persons—scholars and popularizers alike—can come forward to argue, as though in complete innocence and ignorance of our recent history, that nothing could be more interesting and worthwhile than to sort out the "racial" or "ethnic" components of our thoroughly mongrelized species so as to ascertain the root identity of each and everyone of us. And where to look for that identity if not in our genes?<ref>Ruth Hubbard (June 7, 2006), [http://raceandgenomics.ssrc.org/Hubbard/ Race & Genes]. raceandgenomics.ssrc.org</ref></blockquote>Ruth also became a critic of [[recombinant DNA]] research, in a time when the field was booming. She was concerned that people were attempting to assign every trait, disease, and behavior a genetic cause, leading to an oversimplification of science which does not consider the complexities of nature and outside factors. She termed this craze “genomania.”<ref name=":1" /> She was also worried about the safeguards surrounding such research. In a letter published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science, Hubbard stated that if an epidemic caused by a recombinant organism were to break out, it would be almost impossible to distinguish it from the natural E. coli strains that humans are already exposed to.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=HUBBARD|first=R.|date=1976-09-03|title=Recombinant DNA: Unknown Risks|journal=Science|volume=193|issue=4256|pages=834–836|doi=10.1126/science.193.4256.834-a|pmid=17753611|issn=0036-8075|bibcode=1976Sci...193..834H}}</ref>

===Commentary on gender and science===
In her essay "Science and Science Criticism," published in 2001 as a chapter of ''The Gender and Science Reader'', Hubbard iterates that she is a scientist and states that "[n]ature is part of history and culture", but not vice versa. She goes on to say that scientists are largely unable to grasp the concept of nature being part of life--- noting how she needed several years to understand the statement. Going into her scientific history, the narrator mentions how she originally never questioned how her efforts fit into society. Narrowing her focus, she exposits that the Vietnam-era women's rights  and [[women's liberation movement]]s helped teach her of the roles of science in society.<ref name=GenderScienceReader/>

She continues forth with the various means of debate for both sides. One notable instance from men is when they revive various old and unfounded biological theories on women to justify the typical subservient positions of the female gender. Hubbard even refers to the means of debate as "breathing new life" into old theories and assumptions. She further exposits the issues revolving around gender equality that were mainly brought to her attention by how she and her colleagues suddenly started getting promoted from their "ghetto" lab positions right into proper titles. She promptly stresses that "[she believes] the subject of women's biology is profoundly political", explaining away the book's title as she does so. Proceeding onward her desire to go beyond "defining [women as a whole] as victims of male power and dominance," and pushes for women everywhere to show independence and individuality while learning to accept and embrace the biology that's continuously used by men to undermine them. To follow up, she goes on to talk about women's health activists re-educating women on the functions of their body and goes on to encourage women to use the re-education to attain great power by eliminating the footholds of male misinformation and misrepresentation of their bodies.<ref name=GenderScienceReader>{{cite book| chapter=Science and Science Criticism |title=The Gender and Science Reader| pages=49–51| author=Ruth Hubbard |editor1=Muriel Lederman |editor2=Ingrid Bartsch |publisher=Psychology Press |year=2001 |isbn=9780415213585}}</ref>

The essay asserts that women scientists must ultimately and paradoxically turn away from the sciences to make their stand against male supremacy as opposed to the many female and [[feminist]] poets, novelists, and artists that can illustrate their points clearly and easily. She notes that politics seems to vanish within the sciences, exemplifying this point by noting social classes aren't a specific category listed under US health studies. The point she makes is that social and political realities can be blended or integrated subtly into all mediums. The subtlety of the integration ultimately creates great difficulty in discerning fact from [[prejudice]]. In addition, artists, novelists, and poets can compose their works without being victim to review under the funding agencies that makes the use of scientific fact tedious and less effective. The author leads in to surmise that the issues around [[women's rights]] must be raised and brought into public focus. After bringing up how science integrates itself into culture, she exemplifies the point by noting the prominence of biological terms in historical terminology and alluringly points out a biologist's tendency to place humanity above all other animals--- not unlike how men view women and their desire for equality. She raises the question of whether or not women can improve the sciences but makes an attempt to bring into attention her belief that women can make an impact. Hubbard closes by saying that scientists never want their work to be forgotten and lost, and that she sides with feminism for political insight and analytic testing on the scientific assumptions about women.<ref name=GenderScienceReader/>

==Personal life==
[[File:Ruth Hubbard and George Wald 1967.jpg|thumb|Hubbard and Wald in 1967]]
Ruth Hubbard was married to WWII GI and fellow Harvard graduate Frank Hubbard in 1942.<ref name="HowStuffWorks" /> Ruth fondly remembered the months that the pair spent traveling via motorcycle across Europe as Frank researched [[harpsichord]]s. The couple divorced in 1951.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mbl.edu/obituaries/ruth-hubbard-wald/|title=Ruth Hubbard Wald|website=www.mbl.edu|access-date=2019-12-06}}</ref>

Ruth had met her second husband, George Wald, while they were both at Harvard. Wald was a Professor of Biology and Ruth’s boss in the research lab. However, the two began and kept their love affair a secret for more than a decade since they were married to other people at the time. After their respective divorces to previous partners, Ruth and George married in 1958.<ref name=":5" /> The couple had two children: a son, musician and music historian Elijah Wald, and a daughter, attorney Deborah Wald.<ref name="dowling2" /> Hubbard would go on to publish a book, ''Exploding the Gene Myth'', with her son Elijah.<ref name=":4" />

Both Ruth and her brother Alexander followed in the footsteps of their activist parents. Alexander Hoffman was a well-known lawyer and activist. Some of his high-profile clients included [[Cesar Chavez]], [[Lenny Bruce]], and multiple members of the [[Black Panther Party]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.berkeleydailyplanet.com/issue/2009-11-05/article/34033?headline=Remembering-Alexander-Hoffman|title=Remembering Alexander Hoffmann. Category: Features from The Berkeley Daily Planet|website=www.berkeleydailyplanet.com|access-date=2019-12-06}}</ref> Like her brother, Ruth Hubbard was an outspoken activist. However, she was not only known for her commentary on science in society but was also as an antiwar and antinuclear war activist, for which she was once arrested on charges of civil disobedience.<ref name=":4" />

Like her second husband, Ruth remained scientifically active until about 1975, and she made an excellent scientific presentation of George Wald's work at a symposium in his honor. George Wald was 17 years older than Hubbard and he died in 1997.
